warmup.q: A worker is inside Thread.sleep(10_000). Another thread calls worker.interrupt(). The worker catches the InterruptedException. Inside the catch block, what does Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() return?
options: true, because it was just interrupted
false, because the flag was cleared when the exception was thrown
warmup.why: Methods that throw InterruptedException clear the interrupt flag first, so inside the catch block the flag already reads false. If the catch only logs, the stop request is gone for good. That's exactly what happened to the relay, and it's why the rule is to rethrow, or to put the flag back with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). The third section takes it line by line.

opening:
Picture a rolling deploy of the payments service. Each old pod should stop in a second or two. One of them takes the full 30 seconds that Kubernetes allows, and then the kubelet kills it. Its shutdown code had asked the outbox relay to stop, then waited for it. The relay, the thread that moves payment events from an outbox table to Kafka, answered with one log line: relay interrupted, carrying on.

The bug behind that line is easy to write. Java makes you catch InterruptedException, and logging it is the quickest way to keep the compiler happy. It even looks responsible. JDK engineers have shipped the same mistake.

In Threads from zero, every thread we started finished on its own. The relay runs until someone tells it to stop, and how to tell it is the question that lesson left open. In this lesson, we'll follow one thread from NEW to TERMINATED, weigh the ways to stop it, and fix the relay so the request isn't lost. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a pod that wouldn't stop and a relay that answered a shutdown request with a log line. We read its state in a thread dump, struck out stop(), daemons and home-made flags, and fixed the relay so the interrupt survives the catch block.

Now search your own code for catch (InterruptedException. Every hit should either rethrow or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). Any hit that only logs is a relay waiting for its deploy.

Next, we'll let two threads update one counter at the same time, and watch it come out wrong with no exception and no warning.

sections.h: Finding out what the relay is doing
sections.html:
Before we fix anything, let's look at the relay the way you would on a stuck pod: in a thread dump. Here it is, taken with jcmd <pid> Thread.print a moment after the lab's relay was interrupted (trimmed):

"outbox-relay" #19 prio=5 os_prio=0 ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping)
        at java.lang.Thread.sleep0(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method)
        at java.lang.Thread.sleep(java.base@21.0.12.1/Thread.java:509)
        at workbench.concurrency.l02.OutboxRelay.run(OutboxRelay.java:39)

The interrupt arrived, the relay printed its line, and it went straight back to sleep. TIMED_WAITING is one of the six values of the Thread.State enum. t.getState() returns the same names that thread dumps print, so learning them once pays off every time you debug a stuck service.

State What the thread is doing
NEW Created, but start() has not been called.
RUNNABLE Running, or ready to run and waiting for a core.
BLOCKED Waiting to enter a synchronized block that another thread holds.
WAITING Waiting with no time limit: Object.wait(), join(), LockSupport.park().
TIMED_WAITING The same with a time limit: sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms).
TERMINATED run() has returned or thrown.

If the waiting states feel abstract, picture someone in an office. BLOCKED is standing at a locked door while somebody else is inside. WAITING is sitting by the phone until it rings. TIMED_WAITING is the same, with an alarm clock set. In Java terms, the locked door is a synchronized block and the alarm is the timeout. The phone call is a notify, an unpark, or the end of the thread you joined.

Three of these states surprise people.

RUNNABLE doesn't mean "using a CPU". The Javadoc says the thread is executing in the JVM "but it may be waiting for other resources from the operating system such as processor." A thread waiting its turn for a core is RUNNABLE. So is a thread stuck in a socket read from Oracle, because the JVM only sees that it's inside native code. A dump full of RUNNABLE threads can still be a service that does nothing, so read the stacks, not just the states.

BLOCKED is only for synchronized. A thread waiting for a ReentrantLock (lesson 7 of this track) is parked instead: the lock's own Java code puts it to sleep with LockSupport.park() until another thread wakes it, and the JVM reports that as WAITING. Search a dump for BLOCKED to find lock contention, and you'll miss every explicit lock.

TERMINATED is final. A thread can't be restarted. If the work must run again, create a new thread, or better, hand the task to a pool.

Our relay spends nearly all of its life in TIMED_WAITING, asleep. So the real question is how one thread can reach into another thread's sleep and tell it to stop. Java has offered more than one answer over the years, so let's weigh them.

try.title: Put a thread in every state
steps: Read ThreadStates below. For each show(...) line, predict the state before you run it.
Run it with the command below and check your predictions.
Find the line the waiter prints when it's interrupted out of wait(). Hold on to it: it explains the relay's bug, and we'll come back to it when we get to interrupts.

code.title: ThreadStates.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** Puts threads into each of the six states and prints what getState() reports. */ public class ThreadStates { static final Object monitor = new Object(); static volatile boolean spin = true; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread sleeper = new Thread(() -> pause(2_000), "sleeper"); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", "before start():", sleeper.getState()); sleeper.start(); show(sleeper, Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING, "inside sleep(2000):"); Thread busy = new Thread(() -> { while (spin) Thread.onSpinWait(); }, "busy"); busy.start(); show(busy, Thread.State.RUNNABLE, "in a busy loop:"); Thread waiter = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { try { monitor.wait(); // no timeout } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("waiter interrupted, flag now " + Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()); } } }, "waiter"); waiter.start(); show(waiter, Thread.State.WAITING, "inside wait():"); Thread blocked = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { } }, "blocked"); synchronized (monitor) { // main holds the monitor... blocked.start(); // ...so this thread cannot enter show(blocked, Thread.State.BLOCKED, "entering a held lock:"); } spin = false; waiter.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked}) t.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked}) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", "after join():", sleeper.getState()); } // getState() is a snapshot, so poll until the thread gets where we sent it static void show(Thread t, Thread.State expected, String label) throws InterruptedException { for (int i = 0; i < 200 && t.getState() != expected; i++) Thread.sleep(10); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", label, t.getState()); } static void pause(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: ThreadStates.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Puts threads into each of the six states and prints what getState() reports. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val monitor = Object() // java.lang.Object, because Kotlin's Any has no wait() @Volatile private var spin = true fun main() { val sleeper = Thread({ pause(2_000) }, "sleeper") println("%-24s%s".format("before start():", sleeper.state)) sleeper.start() show(sleeper, Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING, "inside sleep(2000):") val busy = thread(name = "busy") { while (spin) Thread.onSpinWait() } show(busy, Thread.State.RUNNABLE, "in a busy loop:") val waiter = thread(name = "waiter") { synchronized(monitor) { try { monitor.wait() // no timeout } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("waiter interrupted, flag now ${Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted}") } } } show(waiter, Thread.State.WAITING, "inside wait():") val blocked = Thread({ synchronized(monitor) { } }, "blocked") synchronized(monitor) { // main holds the monitor... blocked.start() // ...so this thread cannot enter show(blocked, Thread.State.BLOCKED, "entering a held lock:") } spin = false val all = listOf(sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked) all.forEach { it.interrupt() } all.forEach { it.join() } println("%-24s%s".format("after join():", sleeper.state)) } // getState() is a snapshot, so poll until the thread gets where we sent it private fun show(t: Thread, expected: Thread.State, label: String) { var i = 0 while (i++ < 200 && t.state != expected) Thread.sleep(10) println("%-24s%s".format(label, t.state)) } private fun pause(ms: Long) { try { Thread.sleep(ms) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } }

try.expect: You'll see NEW, then TIMED_WAITING (in sleep), RUNNABLE (the busy loop), WAITING (in wait()), BLOCKED (main holds monitor, so the new thread can't get in) and finally TERMINATED. The waiter prints waiter interrupted, flag now false. The interrupt woke it, and the flag was cleared on the way out.

sections.h: Weighing the ways to stop a thread
sections.html:
People try four ways to stop a thread like the relay. Let's take them in turn, oldest first.

The oldest is Thread.stop(). It threw an error inside the target thread, wherever that thread happened to be. The thread unwound, released its locks and left half-updated objects behind for other threads to find: half a batch published, say, with the outbox rows not yet marked as sent. It was deprecated in Java 1.2, made to always throw UnsupportedOperationException in JDK 20, and removed in JDK 26. (suspend() and resume() went in JDK 23. Deprecation in Java is a long goodbye.) Old code that still calls stop() fails with NoSuchMethodError on JDK 26 and later. Strike that one.

The second is to make the relay a daemon thread, one the JVM doesn't wait for. When the last non-daemon thread ends, the JVM exits, and daemon threads stop wherever they are. Their finally blocks don't run. A new thread starts with the daemon setting of the thread that created it, so you change it yourself, before start():

Java
Thread relay = new Thread(outboxRelay, "outbox-relay");
relay.setDaemon(true);   // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException
relay.start();
Kotlin
val relay = Thread(outboxRelay, "outbox-relay")
relay.isDaemon = true    // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException
relay.start()            // or: thread(name = "outbox-relay", isDaemon = true) { outboxRelay.run() }

That doesn't stop the relay so much as abandon it. The JVM can cut it off between publishing a message and marking it sent. Daemons suit work you can afford to lose halfway, such as a cache refresher or the metrics flusher in the Try it below. The JVM's own helpers from lesson 1, like Finalizer and Signal Dispatcher, are daemons for the same reason: nobody wants them to hold up an exit. For a relay that moves payment events, strike it too.

The third is a flag of our own: a running field that the owner sets to false and the loop checks on every pass. (It has to be volatile, for reasons the memory model track explains.) It works for a busy loop. But it can't wake a sleeping thread. Our relay would notice only when its current sleep ends, and a thread blocked in queue.take() on an empty queue would never notice at all. The executors you'll soon hand your tasks to don't know about your flag either.

The fourth is interrupt(), and it's the one Java builds on. t.interrupt() sets a flag inside t, called the interrupt flag. If t is blocked in sleep, wait, join or a blocking call such as BlockingQueue.take(), that call wakes up and throws InterruptedException. Otherwise nothing happens right away: the flag stays set until the thread looks at it. This is also how ExecutorService.shutdownNow() stops running tasks.

So cancellation in Java is cooperative, and that's the only kind there is. The interrupt asks. The thread checks, finishes what it's doing, cleans up and returns, at a moment when its data makes sense.

Java can't kill a thread. It can only ask, and the thread stops itself.

So interrupt is the right tool. But our relay was interrupted, and it carried on. Let's find out where the request went.

try.title: Lose a finally block
steps: Run DaemonDemo. Count the flushes, and look for the line from the finally block.
Change setDaemon(true) to setDaemon(false) (in Kotlin, isDaemon = true to false) and run it again. Stop it with Ctrl+C once you've seen enough.
Keep it non-daemon, and add metrics.interrupt(); metrics.join(); just before main's last println. Predict the last two lines, then run it once more.

code.title: DaemonDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. */ public class DaemonDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread metrics = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int i = 1; ; i++) { System.out.println("metrics: flush " + i); Thread.sleep(200); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { System.out.println("metrics: finally block ran"); } }, "metrics-flusher"); metrics.setDaemon(true); // must be called before start(); try false metrics.start(); Thread.sleep(700); System.out.println("main: done, returning"); } }

alt.title: DaemonDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 // A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. fun main() { val metrics = Thread({ try { var i = 1 while (true) { println("metrics: flush ${i++}") Thread.sleep(200) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } finally { println("metrics: finally block ran") } }, "metrics-flusher") metrics.isDaemon = true // must be set before start(); try false metrics.start() // (or: thread(isDaemon = true) { ... }) Thread.sleep(700) println("main: done, returning") }

try.expect: As a daemon, you get four flushes and main: done, returning, and no finally block ran: the JVM exited underneath the thread. As a non-daemon, it flushes forever, because nothing asks it to stop. With the interrupt and the join, it stops at once and prints metrics: finally block ran before main: done, returning. That's what a clean shutdown looks like: ask, then wait.

sections.html:
Here's the part of the relay that answered the shutdown request, straight from the lab's starting code:

Java
// Naive: the interrupt is "handled" by logging it
try {
    Thread.sleep(idleMillis);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    System.err.println("relay interrupted, carrying on");
}
Kotlin
// Naive: the interrupt is "handled" by logging it
try {
    Thread.sleep(idleMillis)
} catch (e: InterruptedException) {
    System.err.println("relay interrupted, carrying on")
}

It looks harmless. The exception was caught and a line was logged. Here's the detail that makes it a bug: methods that throw InterruptedException clear the interrupt flag before they throw. So inside the catch block the flag already reads false, which was the warm-up question. The relay logs, loops round and calls sleep again, and nothing anywhere remembers that someone asked it to stop.

Think of an interrupt as a sticky note on a colleague's monitor that says "please wrap up". If they're asleep at their desk, the note wakes them. If they're busy typing, they see it the next time they look up. The trap is that waking up tears the note off. If they read it, shrug and doze off again, nobody can tell the request was ever made.

So once you've caught the exception, you hold the only copy of the request, and you have two good options. Let the exception propagate, by declaring throws InterruptedException. Or stick the note back on, by restoring the flag before you do anything else:

Java
try {
    Thread.sleep(backoffMillis);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // put the request back
    return;                               // then stop, or throw your own exception
}
Kotlin
try {
    Thread.sleep(backoffMillis)           // Kotlin doesn't force this try, so add it on purpose
} catch (e: InterruptedException) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt()    // put the request back
    return                                // then stop, or throw your own exception
}

Never swallow an interrupt. Rethrow it, or restore it.

If this feels like an easy mistake, you're in good company. JDK 23 fixed ImageIcon.loadImage to restore the flag, and JDK 24 fixed the same bug in FileSystemPreferences.lockFile(). From JDK 26, the Thread Javadoc has a section on interruption that spells out the rule above.

The relay has a second, quieter way to miss the request. When the outbox is full, it publishes batch after batch and never reaches sleep, so no InterruptedException ever arrives. A loop like that must check the flag itself, once per batch, with Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted(). Be careful with the similar-looking static Thread.interrupted(): it reads the flag and clears it, so use it only when you mean to consume the request.

With both fixes in place, the relay stops when it's asked to. The code that asks still has one job left: wait for the relay to finish, and not forever.

try.title: Watch the flag disappear
steps: Run InterruptFlag and read the five numbered lines.
Comment out the line me.interrupt() in the catch block. Predict lines 2 to 5, then run it again.
Explain to yourself why line 4 prints true with the restore in place, and why line 5 then prints false.

code.title: InterruptFlag.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. */ public class InterruptFlag { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); try { Thread.sleep(10_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now " + me.isInterrupted()); me.interrupt(); // restore it: comment this line out and run again System.out.println("2. after interrupt(), flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); } System.out.println("3. isInterrupted() only reads it: " + me.isInterrupted()); System.out.println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: " + Thread.interrupted()); System.out.println("5. so now the flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "worker"); worker.start(); Thread.sleep(200); worker.interrupt(); // a request, not a command worker.join(); } }

alt.title: InterruptFlag.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. fun main() { val worker = thread(name = "worker") { val me = Thread.currentThread() try { Thread.sleep(10_000) // Kotlin doesn't force this try/catch on you } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now ${me.isInterrupted}") me.interrupt() // restore it: comment this line out and run again println("2. after interrupt(), flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } println("3. isInterrupted only reads it: ${me.isInterrupted}") println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: ${Thread.interrupted()}") println("5. so now the flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(200) worker.interrupt() // a request, not a command worker.join() }

try.expect: With the restore: false, true, true, true, false. Line 1 is false because sleep cleared the flag on its way out, and line 2 shows the note stuck back on. Line 4 uses Thread.interrupted(), which reads the flag and clears it, so line 5 is false. Without the restore, every line prints false. The request was lost the moment the exception was caught, exactly as in the relay.

aside.title: Is coroutine cancellation the same thing?
aside.html: Same idea, separate machinery. Cancelling a Kotlin coroutine is cooperative too: delay() and the other suspending functions in kotlinx.coroutines notice it and throw CancellationException. A catch (e: Exception) that swallows that exception can keep a cancelled coroutine running, much like a swallowed interrupt. But cancelling a coroutine doesn't interrupt the thread it runs on. When a coroutine must call blocking code that only listens to interrupts, wrap the call in runInterruptible { }, which turns cancellation into an interrupt. The coroutines track covers this in Cancellation and timeouts.

sections.h: Waiting for the relay to finish
sections.html:
Now look at the other side of the deploy. The shutdown code did the textbook thing: relay.interrupt(), then relay.join(), then close the Kafka producer that the relay publishes with. With the old relay, that join() waited until the kubelet killed the pod. With the fixed relay, it returns as soon as the relay has finished the batch in hand.

You may be thinking, "Why wait at all? Interrupt it and close the producer." Because the relay may still be publishing, and closing the producer under it makes those sends fail. The next idea is usually this one:

Java
// Naive: hopes two seconds is enough
relay.interrupt();
Thread.sleep(2_000);     // "should be enough"
producer.close();
Kotlin
// Naive: hopes two seconds is enough
relay.interrupt()
Thread.sleep(2_000)      // "should be enough"
producer.close()

Thread.sleep(ms) pauses the current thread for at least that long, and promises nothing about any other thread. On a quiet laptop the relay stops within a few milliseconds and the code works. On a node that's busy with three other deploys, it may not. Even when the relay has finished, the shutdown code isn't promised to see what it wrote. The language gives sleep no synchronization meaning, so the JIT may compile each thread as if the other didn't exist: it can keep a value in a register instead of memory, or move a read or a write. The memory model track shows a loop that never ends for exactly this reason.

join() fixes both problems. It waits for the thread to end, and when it returns, you're guaranteed to see everything that thread wrote. The java.util.concurrent docs put it this way: "All actions in a thread happen-before any other thread successfully returns from a join on that thread." Happens-before is the memory model's name for that guarantee. It's also why the lab in Threads from zero could read the partial array after the joins with no locks at all.

The one weakness of plain join() is the one the deploy found: it waits as long as it takes. So give it a limit. join(5_000) waits up to five seconds and returns nothing, so you check relay.isAlive() afterwards. Since JDK 19, join(Duration) returns true if the thread ended:

Java
// Fixed: ask, then wait, but not forever
relay.interrupt();
boolean stopped = relay.join(Duration.ofSeconds(5));   // JDK 19+: true if it ended
if (!stopped) log.warn("outbox relay still running after 5 s");
producer.close();
Kotlin
// Fixed: ask, then wait, but not forever
relay.interrupt()
val stopped = relay.join(Duration.ofSeconds(5))       // JDK 19+: true if it ended
if (!stopped) log.warn("outbox relay still running after 5 s")
producer.close()

A timed join returns as soon as the thread ends, so it costs nothing when the relay behaves. When it says false, you know you stopped waiting before the relay stopped running, and you can log it and decide what to do.

Keep sleep for what it's for: a pause, such as a back-off between retries to the card issuer, or the relay's idle wait between polls. (Since JDK 19 you can write Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(200)), if you like the unit in the type.)

Wait for the thread, not for the clock.

That completes a thread's life. We can start it, read its state, ask it to stop and wait for it to finish. Notice what all of it has in common, though: one thread coordinating with another by hand. None of it says anything about data that two threads change while both are running, and that's where most concurrency bugs live.

try.title: Give up waiting, then wait properly
steps: Read JoinWithTimeout. The worker takes about 500 ms to fetch an FX rate, and main waits for it twice. Predict both printed lines.
Change the timed join to fetch.join(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) and run it again. What does ended say now, and how long did main wait?

code.title: JoinWithTimeout.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; import java.time.Duration; /** join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. */ public class JoinWithTimeout { static long rateCents; // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread fetch = new Thread(() -> { sleepQuietly(500); // stands in for a 500 ms call to an FX-rate service rateCents = 10_842; }, "fx-fetch"); fetch.start(); boolean ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)); // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended System.out.println("after join(100 ms): ended=" + ended + ", alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", rate=" + rateCents); fetch.join(); // no timeout: wait for the end System.out.println("after join(): alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", rate=" + rateCents); } static void sleepQuietly(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: JoinWithTimeout.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import java.time.Duration import kotlin.concurrent.thread // join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. private var rateCents = 0L // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible fun main() { val fetch = thread(name = "fx-fetch") { try { Thread.sleep(500) // stands in for a 500 ms call to an FX-rate service } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } rateCents = 10_842 } val ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended println("after join(100 ms): ended=$ended, alive=${fetch.isAlive}, rate=$rateCents") fetch.join() // no timeout: wait for the end println("after join(): alive=${fetch.isAlive}, rate=$rateCents") }

try.expect: First run: ended=false, alive=true, rate=0, then alive=false, rate=10842. The 100 ms join gave up early, and the plain join waited for the end and saw the rate. With a 2-second limit, ended=true and the rate is already there after about 500 ms. A timed join returns as soon as the thread ends; it doesn't sit out the full time.

compare.title: An interruptible polling loop in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: Thread relay = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); while (!me.isInterrupted()) { // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50); // the compiler forces you to handle the checked exception } catch (InterruptedException e) { me.interrupt(); // restore the flag, so the loop condition sees it } } System.out.println("relay stopped, flag = " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "outbox-relay"); relay.start();

kotlin.title: KotlinRelay.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A polling loop that follows the interruption protocol, in Kotlin. fun main() { val relay = thread(name = "outbox-relay") { val me = Thread.currentThread() while (!me.isInterrupted) { // property syntax for isInterrupted() // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50) // no try/catch is forced on you in Kotlin... } catch (e: InterruptedException) { me.interrupt() // ...but the protocol is the same: restore the flag } } println("relay stopped, flag = ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(300) relay.interrupt() relay.join() println("relay alive after join: ${relay.isAlive}") }

compare.note: The Kotlin version is a direct translation, and the interesting difference is what Kotlin doesn't force on you. It has no checked exceptions, so Thread.sleep(50) compiles with no try at all, and that changes how the bug looks. In Java the usual mistake is a catch that swallows the interrupt. In Kotlin it's often no catch at all: the InterruptedException escapes the lambda, the thread dies with a stack trace on standard error, and any cleanup after the loop never runs. Neither is a clean stop. The protocol is the same in both languages: catch it where you can do something sensible, restore the flag, and leave. isInterrupted reads as a property in Kotlin, and the static Thread.interrupted() still clears the flag.

worked.title: Make a retrying card-issuer call cancellable

steps.say: Here's a retry loop of the kind most payment services have somewhere. It calls the card issuer and backs off when the call times out. Read it and find the line where a shutdown request disappears.
steps.code: AuthResult authorize(AuthRequest req) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return issuer.authorize(req); } catch (IssuerTimeoutException e) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { log.warn("interrupted during back-off", ie); // and loop again } } } }

alt.html: fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): AuthResult { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return issuer.authorize(req) } catch (e: IssuerTimeoutException) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { log.warn("interrupted during back-off", ie) // and loop again } } attempt++ } }

steps.say: It's the inner catch. sleep cleared the flag before it threw, so after the log line nothing remembers the request, and the loop has no limit. If the issuer is down during a rollout, this thread retries until the pod is killed. It's the relay's bug in a different place. Before you read on, decide what the method should do when it's interrupted.

Put the request back first, then stop retrying and tell the caller why. Wrapping the cause in your own exception is fine, as long as the flag is set before you throw. And while we're here, let's give the retries a limit.
steps.code: AuthResult authorize(AuthRequest req) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return issuer.authorize(req); } catch (IssuerTimeoutException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // 2. restore the request throw new AuthCancelledException(req.id(), ie); // 3. stop, and say why } } } }

alt.html: fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): AuthResult { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return issuer.authorize(req) } catch (e: IssuerTimeoutException) { if (attempt == 3) throw e // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // 2. restore the request throw AuthCancelledException(req.id, ie) // 3. stop, and say why } } attempt++ } }

steps.say: Now the caller, say an executor that is shutting down, finds the interrupt flag still set on its worker thread, and the payment is reported as cancelled instead of being retried forever. If authorize could simply declare throws InterruptedException, that would be simpler still: there would be nothing to restore.

lab.title: Make the outbox relay stop on interrupt
steps: Run the tests. All five fail, and the run is slow, because each test waits 5 seconds for a relay that never stops. This is the relay from the deploy.
Read OutboxRelay.run(). Find the two ways it ignores an interrupt: while sleeping, and while busy with full batches.
Change the loop condition so it checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() once per batch. Finish the batch in hand before checking.
Handle the InterruptedException from sleep by restoring the flag and leaving the loop.
Run the tests until all five pass, then run them once more.
hints: Put the try around the whole while loop. Then the catch block runs once, restores the flag, and run() returns.
If the loop ends because isInterrupted() returned true, the flag is still set. You only need to restore it after an InterruptedException.
The "finishes the batch" test counts messages: the total must be a multiple of the batch size. Don't check the flag inside the for loop over the batch.

drill.title: Write an interruptible poller from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a Runnable that polls a Supplier<List<String>> and prints each item. When the list is empty, it sleeps 100 ms. It must stop when interrupted, whether it's sleeping or busy, and leave the flag set when it returns. Then compare with the answer.

answer.html: Runnable poller = () -> { try { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { List<String> batch = source.get(); batch.forEach(System.out::println); if (batch.isEmpty()) Thread.sleep(100); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // sleep cleared it; put it back } };

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: val poller = Runnable { try { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { val batch = source.get() batch.forEach(::println) if (batch.isEmpty()) Thread.sleep(100) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // sleep cleared it; put it back } }

recap: A thread is NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING or TERMINATED. RUNNABLE also covers waiting for a core and sitting in native I/O, so read the stack as well as the state.
BLOCKED is only for a synchronized monitor. A thread parked on a ReentrantLock shows WAITING.

Java can't kill a thread (Thread.stop() was removed in JDK 26), and a daemon is abandoned, not stopped. interrupt() sets a flag, and blocking calls like sleep, wait, join and take throw InterruptedException and clear it.
When you catch InterruptedException, rethrow it or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). A loop that never blocks must check isInterrupted() itself.
join() waits for a thread to end and makes everything it wrote visible to you; give it a timeout when the wait must end. sleep() only passes time.
The limit: start, interrupt and join coordinate one thread with another. They don't protect data that two running threads change at the same time.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "Why can't I just catch InterruptedException and log it? The thread keeps working, so what's the harm?" Answer them in your own words.
explain.answer: An interrupt is how the rest of the system asks your thread to stop: executors, shutdown code and frameworks all use it. When sleep or wait throws InterruptedException, it clears the interrupt flag first. If you only log, the request is gone, and nobody above you can tell it was ever made. So the loop keeps running, and shutdown hangs until the process is killed, just like the outbox relay during the deploy. Either let the exception propagate, or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to put the flag back, then stop what you're doing.

deeper.html:
Not every blocking call listens to interrupts, and it's worth knowing which ones don't before you meet them in production.

sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take and Lock.lockInterruptibly throw InterruptedException. A thread blocked on an NIO InterruptibleChannel gets different treatment: the Javadoc says the channel is closed, the flag is set and the thread receives a ClosedByInterruptException. So interrupting a thread that is writing to a FileChannel closes the file for everyone who shares that channel. That one surprises people.

Plain synchronized doesn't respond at all. A thread that is BLOCKED waiting for a monitor stays blocked when you interrupt it; only the flag changes. A platform thread reading a classic java.net.Socket stream may also sit there until data arrives. For those, give the wait a timeout (a socket read timeout, or tryLock with a timeout), so the thread wakes up now and then and can check its flag.

Two smaller facts to finish. Interrupts are part of the memory model too: if T1 interrupts T2, everything T1 did before the interrupt is visible to T2 once T2 sees it, by catching the exception or by reading the flag. And the JDK 27 Javadoc for interrupt() notes that interrupting a thread that isn't alive still records the request in the reference implementation, so don't count on an interrupt sent before start() being dropped.
